spans.s:
Eta in the plural (etāḥ) denotes the steeds of the Maruts, being a swift species of deer, which are mentioned several times in the Rigveda, and the skins of which are also said to be worn by the Maruts on their shoulders. The epithet pṛthubudhna, once applied to them in the Rigveda, and variously interpreted as ‘broad-hoofed,’ ‘broad-chested,’ and ‘broad in the hinder part,’ seems to indicate that they were not gazelles.
Foot notes i. 165. 2; 169, 6, 7; v. 54, 5; x. 77. 2.
Rv. i. 166, 10. Cf. Roth, St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
i. 169. 6.
By Grassman and Zimmer.
Griffith, Hymns of the Rigveda, 1, 235.
Monier-Williams, Dictionary, s.v.
Cf. Zimmer, Altindisches Leben, 83.

1. Etaśa is in several passages of the Rigveda, according to Roth the name of a protégé whom indra helped against the sun-god sūrya. But in all these passages etaśa seems merely to designate the horse of the sun.
Foot notes i. 62, 15; iv. 30. 6; v. 29. 5.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v.
Macdonell, Vedic Mythology, pp. 149. 150.

2. Etaśa is in the kauṣītaki brāhmaṇa the name of a sage who is said to have cursed his children because they interrupted him in the midst of a rite; hence the Aitaśāyanas (descendants of etaśa) are declared to be the worst of the Bhṛgus. The same story appears in the aitareya Brāhmaṇā where, however, the sage's name is aitaśa, and the Aitaśāyanas are described as the worst of the Aurvas.
Foot notes xxx. 5.
vi. 33. Cf. Hillebrandt. Vedische Mythologie, 2, 173.
